paragraphs.text: The Applicants seek judicial review of a March 12, 2025 decision [Decision] by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, confirming the finding of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] that the Applicants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [Act].

In particular, the RAD confirmed the RPD’s findings that the Applicants’ claims of being Khalistan supporters and fearing persecution by the authorities in India lacked credibility, and that an internal flight alternative [IFA] existed for the Applicants in the city of Mumbai. The RAD particularly found that the Applicants had not advanced evidence establishing that their alleged agents of harm were motivated to track and harm them throughout the country, and in the proposed IFA. It also noted that as the Applicants had conceded the second prong of the IFA test, that it would be reasonable for them to relocate to the IFA, the central question in their matter was whether the first prong of that test was satisfied, that is, whether the IFA was safe.

The Applicants allege that the RAD’s decision was unreasonable, stating that it erred in its assessment of the agent of harm’s means and motivation to locate them in the proposed internal flight alternative. They also state the RAD erred as it failed to consider the reasonableness of the proposed IFA.
For the following reasons, this application is dismissed. I find the Applicants have not established that the Decision is unreasonable.

The Applicants are citizens of India who allege that they fear persecution from the Punjabi police, because the authorities believe that they support Sikh militants. They state this is because the Principal Applicant, Mr. Singh, had once helped someone find a job, only to later learn that the person was a suspected Sikh militant. The Applicants state that they were subsequently detained and assaulted on multiple occasions by the police, who released them only after the payment of bribes. The Applicants also state that after they fled to Canada, and sought asylum, they became supporters of Khalistan.

The RPD rejected the Applicants’ claim, holding that they had a viable IFA in the city of Mumbai. In light of the evidence before it, the RPD concluded it was unlikely that the police would be motivated to pursue, locate and seek to harm the claimants throughout India. It also found that the Applicants claim that they have become Khalistan supporters after coming to Canada were not truthful and credible.

The RAD performed its own assessment of the evidence and dismissed the appeal, in a Decision dated March 12, 2025. It came to similar conclusions as the RPD, determining that the Applicants would not face the requisite risk of harm in Mumbai, finding that the evidence did not establish that the police would be motivated to seek and harm the Applicants in that city. The RAD further found that that the Applicants’ claim of becoming Khalistan supporters while in Canada was not credible. Accordingly, it found that the Applicants were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The issue at play in this matter is whether the decision under review is reasonable.
paragraphs.heading_before: III. Issues and Standard of Review

paragraphs.text: The parties submit, and I agree, that the applicable standard of review is reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 23 [Vavilov]; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1645 at para 13; Shah v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1741 at para 15). A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85; Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 [Mason] at para 8). Although the party challenging the decision bears the onus of demonstrating that the decision is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 100), the reviewing court must assess “whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility” (Vavilov at para 99; Mason at para 59).

Further, it is the role of administrative decision-making bodies to assess and evaluate the evidence before them. Absent “exceptional circumstances,” a reviewing court should not interfere with a tribunal’s factual findings. The reviewing court must therefore refrain from reweighing the evidence considered by the decision maker (Vavilov at para 125).

The underlying basis for an IFA is the notion that refugee claimants should first seek safety elsewhere in their home country, before seeking protection in Canada. The test for the determination of an IFA is well-established (Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 FC 706 at 711; Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589 at 592). It holds that an individual who faces a risk of harm in one part of a country may only be found to have an IFA in another part of that country if two criteria are met: 1. There must be no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted, or subject to a personalized risk of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual punishment in the part of the country where the IFA exists; and 2. It must not be unreasonable for the claimant to seek refuge in the IFA, considering all of their particular circumstances.

Under the first branch of this test, a serious possibility of persecution, or a risk of torture, risk to life, or risk or cruel and unusual punishment can only be found if it is demonstrated that the agents of harm have both the means and motivation to search for and harm an applicant in the suggested IFA (Saliu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 167 at para 46, citing Feboke v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 155 at para 43; Adeleye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 81 at para 21 [Adeleye]; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 996 at para 8). With respect to the second branch, the threshold to establish unreasonableness is very high, requiring “nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area” (Ranganathan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2001] 2 FC 164, 2000 CanLII 16789 (FCA) at para 15). Once an IFA is proposed, the onus is on the claimant to prove that they do not have a viable IFA (Olusola v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 799 at para 9; Adeleye at para 20). V. Analysis A. The RAD’s decision is reasonable

At the outset, I must note that the written submissions of counsel for the Applicants were, to put it charitably, rather muddled, confused and difficult to parse. Even more concerning, these submissions clearly contain arguments that are made in relation to findings that were never actually made by RAD in its Decision. For example, in the Decision the RAD is clear in setting out that it did not need to address the issue of whether the agents of harm possessed the means to locate and harm the Applicants in the proposed IFA, since the evidence established that those parties lacked the motivation to do so. The RAD accordingly made no determinations with respect to means in its reasons. However, the submissions of the Applicants inaccurately declare that the RAD had found that the Indian police lacked the means to track and strike at the Applicants in Mumbai, and confoundingly went on to argue, at some length, as to why the Court should find this determination to constitute a reviewable error. There are a series of such misplaced arguments in the Applicants’ written submissions, which counsel for the Applicants specifically stated that he continued to rely upon during the hearing of this matter. As a result, I am compelled to note that the indiscriminate use of boilerplate or recycled submissions in counsel materials is not only unhelpful to the Court but can be detrimental to both the professional reputation of the author, and worse, the interests of their client.

In any event, as best as can be discerned from the materials and oral submissions of counsel for the Applicants, the following two central arguments have been advanced. First, that the RAD erred in its finding that the agents of harm lack the motivation to pursue the Applicants nationwide, because the evidence shows that the police have periodically gone to the home of the Applicants searching for them. I note that the RAD directly addressed this argument in its Decision, as it determined that, to the extent that there was any evidence indicating that the police were searching for the Applicants, that evidence indicated that they were only searching for the Applicants locally, rather than outside of the Punjab. The RAD particularly noted the evidence of the police approaching the Applicants’ home in this analysis, pointing out that their home was in the Punjab. The RAD then specifically accepted that the police visits to the home did weigh in favour of finding that there was some motivation to find them outside of the Punjab, but concluded that this was not sufficient to indicate that they were likely motivated to seek to locate or harm the Applicants in Mumbai. In coming to this determination, the RAD noted that the effort required for the agents of harm to locate the Applicants nationwide, throughout the vast and populous country of India, would be much greater than that required to search for them at the known local address of their home in Kala Sanghian.

At best, the Applicants’ argument in this regard amounts to a disagreement with the RAD’s determination and weighing of this evidence and a request for the Court to reweigh it and come to a more favourable conclusion. However, on judicial review, it is not the role of the Court to reevaluate or reweigh the evidence considered by the decision maker (Vavilov, at para 125). It is rather to consider whether the challenged decision exhibits the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency, and to intervene only where there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that the rationale of why the decision was made cannot be understood (Vavilov at paras 85-86, 100). I do not find that to be the case with respect to the RAD’s determination as to the local character of the searches for the Applicants, and I do not find that the RAD erred in its assessment of the agent of harm’s motivation, as a result.

The second argument raised by counsel for the Applicants in oral submissions was that the RAD had erred as it failed to address the second prong of the IFA test, the question of the reasonableness of the Applicants relocating to the proposed IFA. Counsel argues that while the RAD spent considerable effort in discussing the issues of credibility and motivation, it did not deal with the issue of reasonableness and “could have at least spent a few lines of the decision” on this matter. It is clear from the Decision, however, that the RAD did not fail to address this issue. Though the RAD does not say a great deal about the reasonableness prong of the IFA test, it notes the Applicants and their representative had conceded that issue before the RAD, directly admitting that it would not be unreasonable in all of the circumstances for them to relocate to Mumbai. The RAD then went on to state that irrespective of this, it had nonetheless reviewed the RPD’s determination with respect to reasonableness and that it both agreed with and adopted the RPD’s reasoning in this regard. Finally, I note that beyond baldly and erroneously stating that the RAD had failed to address the second prong of the IFA test, the Applicant made no submissions identifying any specific issues or errors in the RPD’s (and thus RAD’s) reasonableness analysis. I do not find that the RAD somehow erred in this regard.

In short, I do not agree that the RAD’s Decision was unreasonable for any of the reasons raised by the Applicant. There is a clearly a discernable rational chain of analysis in the RAD’s findings that is, “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85). I find the RAD undertook a thorough and rigorous independent assessment of the evidence, and further that the Decision is reasonable.

This application for judicial review is dismissed. The parties proposed no question for certification, and I agree that none arises.
